page.h1: HTS Chapter 08: Edible Fruit and Nuts — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Chapter 08 Export Rules: Shipping U.S. Fruit & Nuts Abroad
seo.shortDescription: What the U.S. requires before you export almonds, pistachios, walnuts, apples, grapes and other fruit: Schedule B, phytosanitary certificates, the Export Apple and Grape Acts, licences and AES, plus ways to pay less abroad.

intro: Shipping fruit and nuts out of the U.S. is routine on the paperwork side: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file the export in AES. Fruit and nuts are EAR99, so no Commerce licence applies in the ordinary case. What takes work is plant health and quality. Most buyers want a **USDA APHIS phytosanitary certificate** for fresh fruit, and many set orchard, packing-house or treatment conditions in a bilateral work plan. Two old U.S. laws add a federal grade inspection before export: the **Export Apple Act** for apples and the **Export Grape and Plum Act** for table grapes. Nuts bound for the EU usually carry an aflatoxin certificate from a USDA-run pre-export testing program, and nut and dried-fruit plants selling to China must be registered with China's customs agency.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Tree nuts dominate: almonds are 0802.11 (in shell) and 0802.12 (shelled), pistachios 0802.51 and 0802.52, walnuts 0802.31 and 0802.32. Fresh apples are 0808.10, table grapes 0806.10, strawberries 0810.10, oranges 0805.10 and sweet cherries 0809.29. The first six digits are the HS code on the Overview.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Nuts often move through traders and regional hubs such as the UAE and Hong Kong. Screen the consignee and, where you know it, the final buyer.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Fresh, dried and frozen fruit and nuts are EAR99, so no Commerce licence is needed unless the destination or end user is restricted (see the sanctions step).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Food sales to Cuba are allowed only under the Trade Sanctions Reform Act (cash in advance or third-country bank financing, with prior notice to BIS under License Exception AGR), and OFAC general licenses cover most food sales to Iran. Check the current OFAC program before quoting a sanctioned destination.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: A container of nuts or fresh fruit is almost always worth more than $2,500 per Schedule B number, so plan to file in AES.

rules.title: Phytosanitary certificate: the U.S. does not require one, but most buyers' plant-quarantine agencies do for fresh fruit, and many do for raw nuts. An APHIS or authorized state inspector inspects the lot and issues the certificate (PPQ Form 577) through APHIS's PCIT system. APHIS's Phytosanitary Export Database (PExD) lists, country by country, the additional declarations, treatments (cold treatment or fumigation) and registered orchard or packing-house programs each buyer requires; China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and India set fruit-specific work plans.

citations.label: PCIT and PExD (Phytosanitary Certificate Issuance and Tracking)

rules.agency: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), Specialty Crops Inspection
rules.title: Export Apple Act: fresh apples shipped to any foreign destination must grade at least U.S. No. 1 (or U.S. No. 1 Early), be free of apple maggot within the stated tolerances, be marked with the packer, variety and grade, and be inspected and certified by the Federal or Federal-State Inspection Service. The carrier keeps a copy of the “Export Form Certificate”. Exempt: up to 5,000 lb (100 boxes) per conveyance, processing apples marked “Cannery”, and apples shipped to Canada in bulk containers.

citations.label: 7 CFR 33.10–33.12 (Export Apple Act requirements and exemptions)

rules.agency: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), Specialty Crops Inspection
rules.title: Export Grape and Plum Act: vinifera table grapes must be inspected within 14 days before export and certified as meeting U.S. Fancy grade for Japan, Europe and Greenland, or U.S. No. 1 for other destinations, with each package marked with the grower or packer, variety and lot stamp. Shipments to Canada and Mexico are exempt from the inspection and marking requirements.

rules.agency: USDA AMS (Laboratory Approval Service) with the Almond Board of California and the Administrative Committee for Pistachios
rules.title: Aflatoxin pre-export testing for the EU: AMS approves the laboratories that test almonds bound for the EU under the Almond Board of California's Pre-Export Check (PEC) program, and pistachios under the Pistachio Export Aflatoxin Reporting (PEAR) program, and administers the testing. U.S. law does not require it, but EU buyers expect a PEC or PEAR result with each lot because the EU enforces strict aflatoxin limits at the border.

rules.agency: General Administration of Customs of China (GACC), with the U.S. competent authority
rules.title: China facility registration: since June 1, 2026 GACC Decree No. 280 (which replaced Decree No. 248) requires plants that make nuts and seeds or dried fruit for China to be registered with GACC before export, on the recommendation of the exporting country's competent authority after an audit. Registration runs five years and is filed through GACC's CIFER single window; GACC charges no fee. Fresh fruit is handled instead through APHIS–GACC protocols with registered orchards and packing houses (see PExD).

citations.label: Singapore Food Agency circular on GACC Decree No. 280 (July 28, 2026)

groups.label: Coconuts, Brazil nuts & cashews
groups.note: Small U.S. trade, mostly re-exports. A phytosanitary certificate when the buyer asks for one.

groups.label: Other nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, pistachios, pecans…)
groups.note: Raw nuts need a phytosanitary certificate for many buyers (not the EU). EU shipments carry PEC (almonds) or PEAR (pistachios) aflatoxin results, and plants selling to China must be GACC-registered.

groups.label: Bananas & plantains
groups.note: Mostly re-exports of imported bananas to Canada. APHIS issues a phytosanitary certificate for re-export (PPQ Form 579) on request.

groups.label: Dates, figs, pineapples, avocados, guavas & mangoes
groups.note: Avocados, dates and pineapples, largely to Canada. A phytosanitary certificate where the buyer requires one.

groups.label: Citrus fruit
groups.note: Citrus usually needs a phytosanitary certificate with additional declarations (for example on citrus canker or fruit flies) and, for some buyers, an approved export program. Check PExD for the destination.

groups.label: Grapes & raisins
groups.note: Table grapes need an AMS inspection under the Export Grape and Plum Act (except to Canada and Mexico) and usually a phytosanitary certificate. Raisins need neither in most markets.

groups.label: Melons, watermelons & papayas
groups.note: Melons go mostly to Canada. A phytosanitary certificate where the buyer requires one.

groups.label: Apples, pears & quinces
groups.note: Apples need an Export Apple Act inspection (at least U.S. No. 1) for every foreign destination except small lots, processing apples and bulk bins to Canada, plus a phytosanitary certificate for most buyers.

groups.label: Apricots, cherries, peaches, plums
groups.note: Cherries and other stone fruit for Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China ship under bilateral protocols (treatments, registered orchards and packing houses). Check PExD for the destination.

groups.label: Other fresh fruit (berries, kiwifruit, tropical fruit)
groups.note: Berries go mostly to Canada. A phytosanitary certificate where the buyer requires one.

groups.label: Frozen fruit & nuts
groups.note: Frozen fruit is a processed product: no agency rule beyond the steps in most markets, though some buyers ask for a health certificate.

groups.label: Dried fruit (prunes, apricots…) & mixtures
groups.note: Plants making dried fruit for China must be registered with GACC under Decree No. 280.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Use the EU's duty-free quota for U.S. tree nuts
savings.saves: The EU's normal duty on tree nuts (for example 5.6% on in-shell and 3.5% on shelled almonds) on U.S. nuts entered within a 500,000-tonne yearly quota.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin nuts of CN 0802 and prepared nuts of CN 2008.19 shipped to the EU, from July 1, 2026.
savings.document: The EU importer declares the quota preference (code 320) with U.S. origin and proves non-preferential U.S. origin (document code U190), for example by showing the goods came directly from the U.S. or stayed under customs supervision in transit.
savings.caveat: The quota is first come, first served and runs in 12-month periods from July 1; once it is used up the normal duty applies. The preferences end on December 31, 2029 unless renewed, and the Commission can suspend them.

citations.label: Access2Markets: EU duties on U.S. goods from July 1, 2026

savings.title: Have your Chinese buyer use China's tariff exclusion process
savings.saves: China's 2018–19 counter-tariffs answering U.S. Section 301 (25% or more on U.S. fruit and nuts), which apply on top of everything else when the buyer holds no exclusion.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. fruit and nuts imported into China by a buyer whose exclusion covers the goods.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies under China's market-based exclusion process; the U.S. exporter supplies the product and origin details.
savings.caveat: Exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026, with no extension announced. They do not remove China’s 15% 2018 counter-tariff or its extra 10% on all U.S. goods.

citations.label: White House fact sheet on the U.S.–China deal (Nov 1, 2025)
Tariff Commission Announcement No. 5 of 2018 (2018 list)

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
